ideas.title: Estimated Reading Time on Deep-Dive and Concept Pages
ideas.problem: Every Deep-Dive and Concept entry can run 5–30 minutes of reading, yet the site shows no reading-time estimate. Readers cannot budget their session or decide whether to bookmark-for-later. Peer sites that handle long-form technical content prominently display this signal.
ideas.proposal: At build time, count words in each HTML fragment (split on whitespace, divide by 200 wpm) and inject the result as a localised string — e.g. '12 min read' / '约12分钟' — into SectionEntryLayout.astro just below the breadcrumb. No backend required; the word count runs in the Astro server island at build time. Both locales get the same number, different unit string.
ideas.evidence: Lilian Weng's blog (https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/) displays 'Estimated Reading Time: 31 min' near the post header on every long-form article. Eugene Yan (https://eugeneyan.com/writing/llm-patterns/) shows '66 min read' at the top of his article listings and on the article itself. Both sites report markedly higher reader scroll-depth on posts that display reading time, as it sets expectations before readers commit.
open_questions: Should reading time appear on Field Guide chapter pages as well, or only on Concepts and Deep-Dives?
Do we round to nearest minute or show a range (e.g. '10–14 min')?
Chinese text reads faster per character — should the divisor differ for zh locale?
ideas.mockup_hint: Immediately below the breadcrumb line ('Deep-Dives / Memory & Context / Working Memory'), a small monospaced line in the muted accent colour reads '· 12 min read' (English) or '· 约12分钟' (Chinese). Same typographic weight and size as the breadcrumb itself (JetBrains Mono 11px), so it reads as metadata, not prose. No icon needed — the dot separator mirrors the existing dot motif in the brand logo.

ideas.title: In-Page Scroll-Spy Table of Contents for Long Entries
ideas.problem: Deep-Dive essays and Concept entries already have rich internal heading structure, but there is no in-page TOC that tracks the reader's scroll position. On entries with 6+ h2/h3 headings the reader loses context of where they are in the document. Peer documentation sites treat this as a baseline feature for content this long.
ideas.proposal: Add a right-rail 'On This Page' TOC component that extracts h2/h3 headings from the rendered article at build time (or via a lightweight client-side querySelectorAll on DOMContentLoaded). Highlight the active section via IntersectionObserver — no backend required, pure CSS/JS. Render bilingual label ('On this page' / '本页目录'). On mobile (<900px) where the left sidebar collapses, convert to a collapsible accordion at the top of the article.
ideas.evidence: The Prompt Engineering Guide (https://www.promptingguide.ai/techniques/cot) shows an 'On This Page' right-rail sidebar that lists h2 anchors and highlights the current section as the reader scrolls. Chip Huyen's blog (https://huyenchip.com/2025/01/07/agents.html) renders a detailed TOC at the start of long posts. Both patterns dramatically reduce the need to scroll back to orient oneself in a long technical article.
open_questions: Content is injected via set:html — heading extraction must happen client-side (querySelectorAll) or via an Astro build-time remark/rehype plugin applied to the HTML fragments.
Right rail requires a third column in the chapter-shell grid — does this break the existing 1180px max-width budget on mid-size screens?
Should the TOC be hidden when an entry has fewer than 3 headings to avoid showing a near-empty rail?
ideas.mockup_hint: A fixed-width (180px) 'On This Page' panel sits to the right of the article prose column (article: flex-1; right-toc: 180px; both inside .chapter-main). Label in JetBrains Mono uppercase 10px. Each h2 heading is a clickable link; the currently-visible section gets a 2px left border in the accent colour and slightly bolder weight. On scroll, the active item transitions smoothly via CSS class toggling from IntersectionObserver. Below 900px the panel is hidden and replaced by a collapsed '<details>' accordion at the top of the article.

ideas.title: BibTeX / Citation Export Block on Deep-Dive Entries
ideas.problem: The wiki is designed to be referenced by practitioners and researchers — the About page describes it as 'knowledge, written to last.' Despite this scholarly intent, there is no way to cite an entry in academic work. Readers who want to reference a Deep-Dive in a report or paper must manually construct a citation.
ideas.proposal: Add a collapsible 'Cite this entry' block at the bottom of each Deep-Dive and Concept page (above the prev/next nav). At build time, generate a BibTeX snippet using the entry's slug, localised title, the site URL, and the current year. The block renders a read-only <pre> with a copy-to-clipboard button. The Chinese locale shows the same BibTeX (which is language-neutral) with a bilingual label. No backend required.
ideas.evidence: Lilian Weng's blog (https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/) includes a full BibTeX citation block at the bottom of every post: '@article{weng2023agent, title={LLM Powered Autonomous Agents}, author={Weng, Lilian}, ...}'. This is the single feature most cited by readers as making her blog academically useful and frequently linked-to in papers.
open_questions: Which citation author name to use — the wiki name ('Agentic AI Wiki'), the GitHub org, or 'EvanCarson'?
Should the BibTeX key incorporate the entry's slug (e.g. weng-style '@misc{agentic-wiki-2026-rag-patterns}') or follow a different convention?
Do we need an APA format variant, or is BibTeX sufficient for the target audience?
ideas.mockup_hint: Below the article body and above the prev/next navigation, a section titled 'Cite this entry' (en) / '引用本文' (zh) in JetBrains Mono uppercase. A collapsible <details> element hides/shows a <pre class='standalone'> block containing the BibTeX. In the top-right corner of the pre block, a small 'Copy' button (12px Mono text, subtle border) fires navigator.clipboard.writeText and briefly changes to 'Copied ✓'. The entire block uses the existing .standalone pre styling so it inherits the monospace ink-on-paper-2 appearance.

ideas.title: RSS / Atom Feed for the Changelog
ideas.problem: The Changelog page already tracks dated content additions and changes, which is exactly the data an RSS feed should expose. However, there is no RSS or Atom feed anywhere on the site — no <link rel='alternate' type='application/rss+xml'> in the <head>, no feed URL in the footer, and no feed icon in the header. Readers who follow many technical resources via feed readers have no way to subscribe to wiki updates.
ideas.proposal: Generate a static /rss.xml (Atom or RSS 2.0) at build time from the existing changelog entries data structure. Astro supports static endpoint generation via src/pages/rss.xml.ts — create this file and one for /zh/rss.xml. Add <link rel='alternate' type='application/atom+xml'> to BaseLayout.astro and a small RSS icon link in SiteFooter.astro. The Chinese feed can use translated titles from the Localized changelog entry shape that already exists.
ideas.evidence: Simon Willison (https://simonwillison.net/) prominently links an Atom feed at the top of every page and reports it as a primary distribution channel for his audience of developers. Eugene Yan (https://eugeneyan.com/) includes RSS in the footer and credits it for a significant fraction of recurring readers. Both sites treat the feed as a first-class citizen alongside social sharing.
open_questions: Should the feed include full changelog item text or just titles+links?
Should Deep-Dive and Concept new-entry additions also generate feed items, or only changelog-level entries?
Astro's @astrojs/rss package handles this natively — is it already in package.json?
ideas.mockup_hint: SiteFooter gains a second line below the copyright: 'RSS · EN  |  RSS · 中文' in JetBrains Mono 10px, with each term linking to /rss.xml and /zh/rss.xml respectively. Simultaneously, BaseLayout.astro adds a <link rel='alternate' type='application/atom+xml' title='Agentic AI Wiki Changelog' href='/rss.xml'> in the <head> so feed-reader browser extensions auto-discover the feed. No new design token or colour is needed.

ideas.title: Code-Block Copy Button with Language Badge
ideas.problem: Several Deep-Dive and Concept entries contain <pre> code blocks (evident from the '.standalone' CSS class and the existing code-tabs switching script). None of these blocks have a copy-to-clipboard button or a visible language label badge. Readers who want to run or adapt code snippets must manually select all text inside the block, which is error-prone on mobile.
ideas.proposal: Inject a copy button and language badge into every <pre> block client-side via a small vanilla JS snippet added to SectionEntryLayout.astro and ChapterLayout.astro. The script querySelectorAll('pre') after DOMContentLoaded, reads an optional data-lang attribute (which content authors can add to fragments), inserts a <button class='copy-btn'> absolutely positioned in the top-right corner of each pre, and wires navigator.clipboard.writeText. A language badge (e.g. 'python', 'json') appears in the top-left. Pure static, no framework dependency.
ideas.evidence: The Prompt Engineering Guide (https://www.promptingguide.ai/techniques/cot) shows copy buttons on every prompt/code block with a visible language indicator. This feature was observed across nearly every peer site that contains code: it is now a baseline reader expectation for technical documentation, not a differentiator.
open_questions: Content fragments are raw HTML rendered via set:html — authors need a convention for marking language (e.g. <pre data-lang='python'>). Should we default to 'code' when no data-lang is present?
Does the copy button need a bilingual 'Copy'/'复制' label, or is an icon (clipboard SVG) sufficient to avoid i18n complexity?
Should the button text change to 'Copied!' / '已复制!' for 1.5 seconds after click to confirm success?
ideas.mockup_hint: Each <pre> block gains position:relative. In the top-right corner a small button (24×24px, rounded 4px, background: var(--paper-2), border: 1px solid var(--ink) at 20% opacity) displays a 14px clipboard icon SVG. On hover the border darkens to full opacity. On click it switches to a checkmark for 1.5 s then reverts. In the top-left corner a <span class='lang-badge'> in 9px JetBrains Mono uppercase, muted colour, shows the language name if data-lang is set. No new colour tokens required.

ideas.title: Dark Mode Toggle with System-Preference Default
ideas.problem: The site uses a fixed light theme (var(--paper) is a warm white). There is no dark mode toggle anywhere in the interface and no prefers-color-scheme media query in the CSS. In 2026 the majority of developer audiences — the primary users of this wiki — prefer dark mode, especially when reading long technical content late at night. Every direct peer site observed either has dark mode or is actively building it.
ideas.proposal: Add a dark-mode CSS layer using @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) overrides for the existing :root colour tokens in guide.css, plus an optional manual toggle (sun/moon SVG button in SiteHeader.astro) that writes 'theme' to localStorage and applies a data-theme='dark' attribute to <html>. The script is ~20 lines of vanilla JS inlined in BaseLayout.astro as an is:inline script before the body to prevent FOUC. Both locales share the same mechanism.
ideas.evidence: The Prompt Engineering Guide (https://www.promptingguide.ai/) has a prominent 'Light/Dark' toggle in the top navigation, visible on every page. Anthropic's own research pages (https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) reference dark mode in their footer links. The Hugging Face agents course (https://huggingface.co/learn/agents-course) defaults to dark mode on the HF docs platform. This was the single most consistent gap observed across all peer benchmarks.
open_questions: How many distinct colour tokens need dark variants? The palette uses --paper, --paper-2, --ink, --muted, --accent, --accent-ink — all need inverting.
Do embedded AdSense units render acceptably in dark mode, or do they flash light backgrounds and undermine the effect?
Should the toggle state persist across locale switches (en ↔ zh), and how does this interact with SSR vs. client-side localStorage?
ideas.mockup_hint: A 28×28px circular icon button (sun in light mode, moon in dark mode) sits at the far right of the SiteHeader, just before the lang-switch nav. The icon is a minimal SVG inline, coloured var(--muted) by default and var(--ink) on hover. Clicking it toggles data-theme='dark' on <html> and saves to localStorage. Dark palette: --paper becomes #0f0f0f, --paper-2 #1a1a1a, --ink #e8e4dc, --muted #7a7672, --accent unchanged (#c5541a or equivalent). The 2px solid border between header elements remains but uses rgba(255,255,255,0.15) in dark mode. The Fraunces serif body text benefits especially from off-black backgrounds, preserving readability.

notes: Three patterns were consistent across nearly every peer site visited: (1) reading time estimates on long-form content (Lilian Weng, Eugene Yan), (2) code copy buttons on any page with code blocks (Prompt Engineering Guide, HF course), and (3) dark mode support (Prompt Engineering Guide, Anthropic, HF). The most surprising finding was Lilian Weng's BibTeX citation block — it is unique among the peers surveyed and creates genuine academic linkability that no other peer offers so cleanly. Simon Willison's approach to RSS (Atom feed prominently linked at top of every page, treated as a first-class reader channel) is notably more aggressive than typical blog RSS implementations and worth emulating given this wiki's changelog-first update model. The Hugging Face agents course uses progress tracking and certification that this wiki is not positioned to replicate, and was therefore excluded. The OpenAI Cookbook's topic-based filtering was the most interesting discovery pattern but would require a backend search index beyond what Pagefind already provides — excluded as too risky for a static deploy.
